Q: In python, how should user-editable storage/config that is also changed by the program be handled? A:

TOML is a pretty common format for Python-based configuration files, and it is fairly readable. (You've probably already encountered a pyproject.toml file.) YAML is an extended version of JSON that is also designed to be easier to read and write (for example you can often omit the quotes around strings), but it has a number of syntactic complexities. There are popular libraries on PyPI for both.

JSON happens to share syntax with Javascript but it's very widely used in all languages. As a configuration language it's a little harder to hand-edit, but it has the advantage of being bundled with the standard library. I wouldn't consider it weird at all.

eval() is almost always wrong. Using it at all is a major security exposure, since it allows the configuration file to contain arbitrary code. You'd also have to very carefully escape whatever you write out to make sure you're not accidentally writing the wrong kind of executable thing. A prebuilt (and audited) JSON/YAML/TOML library can handle all of this for you.

Efficiency won't be a concern here. Parsing files (of any sort) isn't that computationally intensive. The disk I/O to read the file won't be free. If your editing UI is network-accessible, the slowest thing in the process will be sending the configuration data across the network and back.
